tip: 'Toda la semana' sounds ongoing, but it's a closed box – the week ended. Bounded durations take preterite: 'estuve', not 'estaba', no matter how long it dragged on.
No 'on' before days – the article does that job: 'los martes' = the Tuesdays = on Tuesdays (every one); 'el martes' alone = this coming Tuesday.
Imperfect ('hablaba') for ongoing action + preterite ('llegó') for interruption.
Who fined you? Just 'they': 'me pusieron una multa' = they put a fine on me. Spanish uses a faceless 'they' where English goes passive (I got fined).
'Por' + a time period = during: 'por las mañanas' (in the mornings), 'por la tarde', 'por la noche'.
Two pasts, two lenses: 'me di una ducha' is the single done event (preterite), 'no tenía mucho tiempo' is the background condition it happened against (imperfect).
'Departamento' looks like 'department', but in Latin America it usually means an apartment. Spain says 'piso' for a flat; context decides office division vs home.
Note it's 'se me fue', not 'fui': the accidental 'se' frames forgetting as something that happened TO you – the saint left on his own, and 'me' marks you as the innocent victim.
Imperfect ('hablaba') for background action + preterite ('se subió') for the sudden event.
'Querer decir' = literally 'to want to say' = to mean. 'No quise decir eso' = I didn't mean that – Spanish treats meaning as what you wanted your words to say.
'Tan... que' = so... that: 'tan bonito que paramos' = so pretty that we stopped. It's 'tan' + adjective + 'que' + the result.
Two pronouns stack: indirect ('le/les') + direct ('lo/la'). 'le' becomes 'se' before 'lo/la' to avoid 'le lo', giving 'se lo dije' = I told it to him.
'Se me olvidó' uses the accidental 'se': it frames forgetting as unplanned, something that happened to you rather than something you did.
Deny a belief and the verb goes subjunctive: 'no creía que fuera posible' uses 'fuera', not 'era'; 'creía que era' means believed it was, while 'no creía' flips the mood.
Here 'llevaba' is imperfect – the scene-setting past for describing people, places, weather, and time.
Two pronouns stack before the verb: 'te' (indirect, to you) + 'lo' (direct, it), giving 'te lo dije' = I told it to you.
'There were more trees,' yet Spanish says 'había', never 'habían': 'había' stays singular no matter how many 'árboles', marking existence, not a plural subject.
'Nos conocimos' isn't 'we knew each other' – 'conocer' in the preterite means MET. Tense flips it: 'conocía' = knew, 'conocimos' = met for the first time.
'Ponerse' is literally 'to put onto oneself' – and because 'me pongo' already says whose body the coat lands on, Spanish uses 'el abrigo', not 'my' coat.
'Hubieras escuchado' (past condition) pairs with 'tendríamos' (present result). Spanish mixes the two when a past mistake still affects the present.
'Poder' in the preterite is loaded: 'no pudimos' means we actually tried to sit together and failed. Imperfect 'no podíamos' would just describe a general inability.
'¿Estás listo?' asks if you're ready – but 'eres listo' would call you clever! 'listo' changes meaning with 'ser'/'estar': 'estar' = the ready-to-go state.
Use 'ser' for events: 'la reunión es a las tres' – events take 'ser' for when and where they happen.
Clothes fit backwards in Spanish: 'me quedaban demasiado grandes' – the pants stayed too big ON me, and 'quedar' works like 'gustar': the garment acts, you receive.
'Me quedé dormido' looks like 'I stayed asleep' but means I FELL asleep – 'quedarse' marks slipping into a new state. That's how you nod off on the bus.
Imperfect for simultaneous past actions: 'mientras ella cocinaba, yo ponía la mesa' – two ongoing actions at once, both in the imperfect.
Here 'vivía' is imperfect: use it for habitual past – repeated actions, routines, and 'used to'.
'Perdona' is the informal attention-getter ('tú' form). Fine for strangers your age; switch to 'perdone' for elders or formal settings – same word, 'usted' ending.
'A pesar de' + infinitive matches English despite + -ing: 'a pesar de ser lunes' = despite being Monday.
Why 'comer' for one specific meal? In Spain 'comer' IS the midday meal – the day's main event, around 2pm, so 'nos invita a comer' = big Sunday lunch, not a bite.
